title: the Vishnu Purana (selections)
tomorrow: who is telling the Prahlada story, and who is listening?

segments.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants ended yesterday on a hymn for a whole room: go together, speak together. Today a new stretch begins, the Puranas, with a boy who says something like that to his whole class.

Some kids say the one thing nobody is supposed to say in front of the teacher. In the Vishnu Purana, that kid is Prahlada. His father is Hiranyakashipu, a demon king who hates the god Vishnu and wants to be worshiped himself. He sends his son to school to learn the king's ways. And Prahlada keeps saying the one thing that can't be said in that palace: Vishnu is in everything. In the trees. In the teacher. In his father. That's the trouble. The king's sworn enemy, found inside the king's own house.
screen: `A KING WHO HATES VISHNU.` → `VISHNU IS IN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: The Vishnu Purana is one of the Puranas, long books of stories about the gods, the world, and how to live in it. One scene in Prahlada's story is easy to miss. The teacher steps out, and Prahlada talks to the other boys, sons of the demon lords. In the Purana's telling, he tells them, roughly: Vishnu is in you, in me, in every being. So let go of enmity. Look on everyone as you'd look on yourself. That's this tradition's answer to an old question: why treat people who are nothing like you as your own? Because the same Lord lives in each of them. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. In the Akal Ustat, a hymn Sikh tradition gives to Guru Gobind Singh, one line says: recognize the whole human race as one. So they share a real thing, a call to see one human family where others see sides. And one honest difference. Prahlada's reason is Vishnu, a god with names and stories, living inside every being. The Akal Ustat's passage looks across people who worship and dress in different ways, praises one timeless Creator, and calls them one kind; it doesn't name that one Vishnu. Prahlada's father doesn't take any of it well. The next chapters are hard ones; this path met one of them at Holi.
screen: `THE PURANAS: BOOKS OF STORIES.` · `PRAHLADA: VISHNU IS IN EVERY BEING.` · `AKAL USTAT: ONE HUMAN RACE.` · `SHARED CALL, DIFFERENT REASONS.` · then, large: `ONE FAMILY WHERE OTHERS SEE SIDES.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand flat on your chest and feel it rise and fall. Bring to mind one person you find hard, and without forcing any warm feeling, hold the plain thought that the same breath moves in them. Keep the hand there until the time runs out.
The Vishnu Purana: a Purana of stories centered on Vishnu, where a schoolboy tells his class that the Lord is in everyone. Today's word.
Your line: the Vishnu Purana, in selections, starting with a boy who saw his whole class as one. New stretch, first day.

howItsDone: Hindus tell Prahlada's story at Holi and in Vaishnava homes and temples, sometimes to children. The Akal Ustat, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, is part of the Dasam Granth. Each tradition keeps its own reasons.

fork.setup: at assembly practice a Sikh senior reads 'recognize the whole human race as one.' a guy behind you snickers. what fits today's lesson?

fork.reveal: Prahlada spoke to his classmates. the Akal Ustat's line and his teaching share a call to one human family, for different reasons; neither is 'all the same'.

notes: First day of 'The Puranas' (Vishnu Purana selections, 1511–1514; 1513–1514 by another writer). Day 141 (Holi) told the fire story; this day takes Prahlada's teaching to his classmates instead, and points to the hard chapters only in one gentle line (for parents: the father's attempts on the boy's life are not narrated).
